hints: Look first at the carbon skeleton and spot where the multiple bonds must be to satisfy carbon's four bonds.
The left end HCC is H-C triple bond C, and the right end CHC(CH3)2 is CH double bond C, so you have one triple and one double bond in total.
Remember every single bond is one sigma, while a double adds one pi and a triple adds two pi, then count all C-C plus C-H sigma bonds.
walkthrough:
**Draw out the structure**

Great start, let's turn the condensed formula into a structure. It is $\text{HC}\equiv\text{C-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH=C(CH}_3)_2$.

That gives 8 carbons and 12 hydrogens in total.

**Count the pi bonds**

This is the easy part. A double bond has 1 $\pi$ bond and a triple bond has 2 $\pi$ bonds.

$$ \pi = 2 \text{ (from C}\equiv\text{C)} + 1 \text{ (from C=C)} = 3 $$

**Count the sigma bonds**

Remember, every bond, single, double or triple, contains exactly one $\sigma$ bond. So count connections.

C-C connections: $7$ $\sigma$ bonds, C-H bonds: $12$ $\sigma$ bonds.

$$ \sigma = 7 + 12 = 19 $$

**Conclude**

Putting it together gives 19 $\sigma$ and 3 $\pi$ bonds, which matches one of the options perfectly.

options.A: Undercounts sigma by 2. This often happens if you miss two C-H bonds on the two CH2 groups or miscount the branched methyl groups.
options.B: Gets pi wrong as 5. This comes from thinking a triple bond has 3 pi bonds, but a triple bond is 1 sigma + 2 pi, not 3 pi.
options.C: Gives 18 sigma and 4 pi. This suggests an extra double bond was imagined or the triple bond was counted as 1 sigma + 3 pi, both are common slips.
options.D: Correct. One C triple bond C contributes 1 sigma + 2 pi, one C double bond C contributes 1 sigma + 1 pi, plus all other C-C and 12 C-H singles give 19 sigma and 3 pi in total.
